Throwing Elbow Injuries
 CORE
August 26, 2026
Brandon Erickson, MD (2020–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Assess the possible causes of elbow injuries in adolescent and adult overhead athletes.
Perform a directed physical examination of the throwing athlete’s elbow.
Outline appropriate imaging modalities to aid in diagnosis.
Compare nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for the various conditions discussed.
Review rehabilitation options after nonsurgical and surgical management.
Assess expected outcomes and potential complications from management of these injuries.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Elbow injuries in throwing athletes have increased in the past 10 years.




NOTES

Despite injury prevention programs and an improved understanding of throwing mechanics,
the incidence of these injuries has continued to rise.
Epidemiology
The number of elbow injuries in throwing athletes of all levels has been increasing for the past
10 years.
Studies have reported that more than 30% of adolescent overhead athletes have reported an
injury at some point during their pitching career.1

Epidemiology
The number of elbow injuries in overhead athletes has been increasing considerably
over the past decade. Despite injury prevention programs, the incidence of these injuries
has been increasing in overhead athletes of all ages and competition levels. For example,
ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) injuries are increasing at an annual rate of approximately
10% per year in adolescent overhead athletes, and approximately 25% of all professional
pitchers have undergone UCL reconstruction (UCLR), also known as Tommy John
surgery2,3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The pitching cycle consists of six phases: the wind-up, early cocking, late cocking, acceleration,
deceleration, and ball release phases4 (Figure 1; Resource 1).
The elbow joint consists of three distinct articulations: the ulnotrochlear, radiocapitellar, and
proximal radioulnar joints.
The UCL consists of three distinct bundles: anterior, posterior, and transverse.
The ulnar nerve, which provides motor and sensory input to the hand, lies posterior to the
medial intermuscular septum before passing around the medial epicondyle and piercing
through the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris.
The inferior ulnar collateral artery provides the intraneural and extraneural blood supply to
the ulnar nerve proximal to the cubital tunnel.

Figure 1
Clinical photographs show the phases of throwing for a baseball pitcher. (Reproduced from
Nissen CW, Solomito MJ: Baseball injuries in adolescents, in LaPrade RF, Kocher MS, Schwarz AJ,

Surgeons, 2016, pp 117-145.)

Anatomy and Biomechanics

3/37

The elbow is one of the more complex joints in the body and is part of the mechanism
that allows overhead athletes to generate a tremendous amount of force to impart on a
ball. Regarding restraints about the elbow, 50% of elbow stability is provided by the
osseous restraints, and soft-tissue restraints, including the flexor-pronator mass, UCL,
and joint capsule, account for the other 50%. The UCL is composed of three bundles. The
anterior bundle is divided into the anterior and posterior bands and provides the most
resistance to valgus stress at the elbow. The anterior bundle originates off the humerus
at the anteroinferior aspect of the medial epicondyle and inserts onto the sublime
tubercle and UCL ridge of the ulna. Most athletes’ elbows sit in some degree of valgus;
however, the amount of valgus may vary considerably. Studies have questioned whether
an increase or decrease in the valgus carrying angle of the elbow contributes to elbow
injuries in throwing athletes; however, no definitive conclusion has been reached.5
Regarding elbow injuries in the throwing athlete, the most common phases of the
pitching cycle to sustain an injury are the late cocking and early acceleration phases.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Often, no singular cause of elbow injuries exists in overhead athletes.
Typically, the injury results from a combination of multiple factors:
Improper pitching mechanics
Throwing with high velocity
Increase in workload
Throwing while fatigued
Other factors
The mechanism of injury may be an acute, traumatic injury, such as a medial epicondyle
fracture, or a chronic, overuse injury, such as valgus extension overload (VEO).

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Elbow injuries in overhead athletes must be understood in the context of the entire
pitching cycle. Although some isolated issues may be present at the elbow (cubital
tunnel), most elbow injuries are the result of several factors, including poor pitching
mechanics and overuse. Although correcting the problem at the elbow may allow a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
4/37

player to successfully return to sport (RTS), it does not correct the etiology of the elbow
problem. Therefore, these athletes are at risk for recurrent injury.
Risk Factors
Several risk factors exist for elbow injuries in overhead athletes.

Risk Factors
Risk factors for elbow injuries in throwing athletes include pitching more than 100
innings per season, pitching on consecutive days, playing pitcher and catcher, growing
up in a warm-weather area, loss of shoulder range of motion (ROM), loss of hip ROM,
pitching with higher velocity, pitching while fatigued, core weakness, and many other
factors. Most injury prevention programs focus on improving pitching mechanics,
increasing shoulder and hip motion, improving scapular mechanics, and improving core
strength.6,7
Associated Injuries
Shoulder injuries are commonly observed in athletes with elbow injuries and vice versa.

Associated Injuries
Associated injuries are common in overhead athletes. One example of an associated
injury in a patient with an elbow injury is shoulder impingement. Shoulder impingement,
which often results from a relative decrease in internal rotation with an increase in
external rotation compared with the contralateral shoulder, may cause pain and loss of
function. This often is managed via stretching programs and scapular stabilization
exercises.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
5/37

Injury Classification
Given the variations in types of injuries, no single injury classification system encompasses all
elbow injuries in throwing athletes.
Specific classification systems are available for some of these injuries, including UCL tears,
olecranon stress fractures, and capitellar osteochondritis dissecans (OCD).

Injury Classification
Injuries of the UCL can be classified based on the location and severity of the tear8
(Resource 2). These can be subdivided into proximal (stage 1), midsubstance (stage 2),
and distal (stage 3) and partial (A) or complete (B). Therefore, a partial distal UCL tear is
classified as a stage 3A tear, whereas a complete proximal UCL tear is classified as a
stage 1B tear. Olecranon stress fractures can be classified as physeal, classic,
transitional, sclerotic, or distal9 (Resource 3). Capitellar OCD lesions typically are
classified similar to other OCD lesions as stable (normal elbow ROM, open capitellar
epiphyseal plate, and lack of fluid between the OCD lesion and the bone on MRI) or
unstable (loss of >20° of elbow ROM, closed capitellar epiphyseal plate, fluid between
the OCD fragment and underlying bone, and fragmentation).
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Several key components of the patient history may aid in diagnosis and help reduce injury in
the future if certain problems are corrected.
These involve gathering information on the cause of injury, timing of injury, duration of injury,
associated injuries, and many other types of information.

Patient History
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
6/37

First, it is important to obtain an understanding of the athlete’s position (pitcher, catcher,
or infielder; play multiple positions, such as pitcher and catcher), workload (play for one
team or three teams, number of innings pitched per game and per season, appropriate
age-based pitching guidelines followed), and level of competition. In addition, surgeons
should determine whether the athlete has sustained a previous elbow injury and, if so,
the manner in which it was managed. Surgeons also must determine whether the
athlete has undergone previous elbow surgery. When and how the injury occurred are
important. Did the injury result from one specific pitch and lead to considerable medial
elbow pain in a skeletally immature patient (eg, medial epicondyle fracture) or did the
injury occur gradually over time? When in the pitching cycle does the arm hurt? Does the
arm hurt during the deceleration phase or during the late cocking/early acceleration
phase (eg, UCL, posteromedial impingement)? Was there a change in speed and/or
control? Was paresthesia, especially of the ulnar nerve, noted?
Next, surgeons must determine the location of elbow pain—medial, lateral, posterior, or
anterior. The elbow is a small area with a number of important structures that cross it;
therefore, understanding the exact location of the pain is important. Surgeons also must
determine if any associated injuries are present. Does the athlete’s shoulder or hip also
hurt? Loss of hip motion or shoulder motion may predispose the player to an elbow
injury and should be corrected for the long-term health of the elbow. Patients with an
elbow injury occasionally present with nerve findings; therefore, surgeons should inquire
about neurologic symptoms that may accompany the injury, including numbness in the
ring and little fingers. Surgeons should ask whether the numbness occurs all the time or
only when throwing. Finally, surgeons must determine if the athlete has undergone prior
treatment for injury. Knowledge of the last time the athlete threw also is important
(recent injury or injury that has been present for an extended period).
Physical Examination
Physical examination of the elbow begins with inspection followed by ROM, strength testing,
palpation, and special tests.
A complete shoulder and neck examination should be performed in these patients because
other factors may be contributing to the injury. Consider discussing core strength and single-
leg stance measurements.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
7/37


Physical Examination
Physical examination begins with inspection of the elbow for bruising, swelling, or
deformity. They elbow is then taken through ROM in flexion, extension, pronation, and
supination. Typically, throwing athletes do not have a loss of flexion, pronation, or
supination but may lose extension secondary to a tight anterior capsule or a
posteromedial osteophyte. Strength is examined next. Resisted elbow flexion and
extension are performed to evaluate for discomfort secondary to biceps or triceps
tendinitis. Resisted wrist flexion and extension and resisted forearm pronation and
supination can be performed to evaluate for lateral epicondylitis (pain with resisted wrist
extension and forearm supination) and medial epicondylitis (pain with resisted wrist
flexion and forearm pronation). Palpation follows the strength examination. Some
surgeons prefer to perform palpation earlier in the physical examination; however, this
may cause the elbow to flare up. The elbow is a relatively small area, and a thorough
understanding of the anatomy of the elbow will allow the examiner to pinpoint the exact
anatomic structure that is painful. Begin with palpation of the lateral epicondyle and the
course of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (pain often indicates lateral epicondylitis).
Next, palpate the radial head and the radiocapitellar joint (pain may be secondary to a
symptomatic plica, osteochondral lesion, or radial head/neck fracture). Next, palpate the
posterior elbow, specifically the olecranon and the triceps tendon, to evaluate for a
persistent olecranon physis, an olecranon stress fracture, or insertional triceps
tendinitis. Finally, move to the medial side of the elbow and palpate the medial
epicondyle (pain on the most prominent aspect often is from a flexor-pronator strain,
medial epicondyle fracture, or medial apophysitis) and along the course of the UCL to
the sublime tubercle.10
Special tests, one of the most important components of the elbow examination, are the
last component of the elbow examination and should be directed based on findings
from the previous parts of the examination. If concern for UCL injury exists, then a static
valgus stress test, moving valgus stress test, and milking maneuver should be
performed. (Figure 2) If concern for posteromedial impingement exists, then a bounce
and arm bar test should be performed. A temple test may help differentiate a UCL tear
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
8/37

from medial epicondylitis.6 Finally, a shoulder and hip examination should be performed
to evaluate for scapular dyskinesis or limitations in shoulder and hip ROM.
Figure 2
Clinical photograph shows the moving valgus stress test. The double-headed arrow indicates the
directions of motion. (Reproduced from Hammond J, Cole BJ: Elbow injuries and the throwing
athlete, in Nicholson GP, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Shoulder and Elbow, ed 4. Rosemont,
IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2013, pp 495-503.)
Neurovascular Examination
An elbow examination in the throwing athlete is not complete without a neurovascular
examination.

Neurovascular Examination
A complete neurovascular examination of the upper extremity should accompany any
elbow examination. This involves assessing sensation of the radial, median, and ulnar
nerves and motor function of the anterior interosseous nerve, posterior interosseous
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
9/37

nerve, and ulnar nerve. In overhead athletes, the most commonly injured/irritated nerve
is the ulnar nerve. This typically occurs at the level of the elbow. To completely examine
the ulnar nerve, surgeons should assess for ulnar nerve subluxation by placing a finger
on the medial epicondyle and passively flexing and extending the elbow to determine if
the ulnar nerve subluxates over the medial epicondyle. An ulnar nerve compression test
at the elbow and a Tinel test of the ulnar nerve at the elbow also should be performed.
Physical examination is extremely important for evaluation of the ulnar nerve because
MRI often may demonstrate increased signal intensity of the ulnar nerve in
asymptomatic patients. Therefore, surgeons must determine whether this imaging
finding is normal or abnormal based on physical examination findings.11
The radial nerve also should be examined for signs of compression. Patients with radial
tunnel syndrome (also known as Wartenberg syndrome) experience forearm pain that
radiates down to the dorsum of the thumb. Forearm pronation and ulnar deviation of
the wrist and percussion of the forearm approximately 8 cm proximal to the radial
styloid may replicate symptoms. These symptoms occur because the radial sensory
nerve becomes compressed in the interval between the brachioradialis and the extensor
carpi radialis longus. If concern for potential thrombus or thoracic outlet syndrome
exists, then a vascular examination is imperative.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Every overhead athlete with elbow pain should undergo a standard three-view elbow series
(AP, lateral, and oblique views; consider axillary elbow view for posterior olecranon
osteophytes).
Often, these radiographs are completely normal.

Radiography
Radiography is used to determine skeletal maturity and to evaluate for any other
osseous abnormalities, such as osteophytes and loose bodies, ossification in the UCL, a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
10/37

sublime tubercle enthesophyte, a persistent olecranon physis, medial epicondyle
fracture, radial head/neck fracture, and other abnormalities. Additional views, including
a 45° internal oblique and distal humerus view, can be obtained if concern for a medial
epicondyle fracture exists. An AP radiograph with the elbow in flexion may be useful in
evaluating for an osteochondral lesion in patients with OCD or VEO. Finally, comparison
radiographs of the healthy elbow may be useful, especially in skeletally immature
patients, to determine whether a finding is abnormal.
Computed Tomography
CT is less commonly performed in the evaluation of throwing elbow injuries than MRI because
many elbow injuries in overhead athletes involve soft-tissue structures.

Computed Tomography
Although CT is not as commonly performed in the evaluation of throwing elbow injuries
as MRI, CT is useful to determine the presence/absence of posteromedial osteophytes
and to evaluate the severity of osteochondral lesions (Resource 4). In addition, CT may
be useful in evaluating for persistent olecranon physis and olecranon stress fractures to
assess for sclerotic bone.12 Finally, CT may be useful to measure displacement in
patients with a medial epicondyle fracture; however, this is not commonly necessary.
Three-dimensional CT reconstructions also may be useful to better characterize these
lesions.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI commonly is the preferred advanced imaging modality for the evaluation of elbow injuries
in throwing athletes.13
Some studies advocate for magnetic resonance arthrography to better define certain
structures, such as the UCL, whereas other studies do not think this imaging modality is
necessary.
Critical evaluation of fluid-sensitive sequences is important to hone in on areas of pathology.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
11/37

Often, a small amount of bony edema will be present in the medial epicondyle, olecranon, or
capitellum, depending on the location of the injury.

Magnetic Resonance Injury
Often, MRI is the preferred imaging modality for overhead athletes with an elbow injury.
It affords excellent visualization of soft-tissue injuries, which are present in most patients
with a throwing elbow injury. One important factor to consider is that MRI findings in
high-level throwers often are abnormal because these players subject their elbows to
considerable amounts of stress during their careers. Therefore, the patient history and
physical examination findings should be considered in combination with MRI findings to
produce an accurate diagnosis. Simply relying on MRI findings for diagnosis often will
result in a misdiagnosis in these athletes because adaptive changes often appear
abnormal on advanced imaging studies.
MRI allows the clinician to evaluate numerous structures about the elbow. The flexor-
pronator mass and the common extensor mass can be evaluated to rule out any type of
epicondylitis or strain. The UCL can be followed from its origin on the medial epicondyle
to the sublime tubercle. On coronal MRIs, the UCL can be closely examined for evidence
of a tear or a T sign. The distal aspect of the UCL is a common site of injury (Figure 3).
Although MRI better defines soft tissue than bony pathology, posteromedial osteophytes
often can be appreciated on MRI. The insertion of the triceps tendon and the olecranon
can be evaluated to assess for triceps tendinitis or an olecranon stress reaction.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM

12/37

Figure 3
Coronal MRI of an elbow shows a distal ulnar collateral ligament tear (arrow). (Courtesy
of Brandon Erickson, MD, New York, NY.)
Bone Scintigraphy
This imaging modality is not commonly performed in overhead athletes.
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography, specifically stress ultrasonography, has become an imaging modality more
commonly performed to evaluate the UCL in overhead athletes13,14 (Resource 5).

Ultrasonography
In the past 10 years ultrasonography has become a more commonly performed imaging
modality to evaluate overhead athletes with an elbow injury. Previous studies reported
that the UCL in throwing athletes often becomes hypertrophic. In addition, studies have
reported more ulnohumeral joint space gapping in players with a UCL injury if the elbow
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
13/37

is stressed compared with individuals with a normal elbow.15 Therefore,
ultrasonography can be performed to track healthy players and diagnose UCL tears in
injured players.
Positron Emission Tomography
This imaging modality is not commonly peformed in overhead athletes.

Posteromedial impingement (Video 1)

Video 1 Savoie FH III, mod: Elbow arthroscopy: Indications, techniques, outcomes, and
complications. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, San Diego, CA, March 14-18, 2017.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Many elbow injuries in throwing athletes can be managed effectively nonsurgically.

Nonsurgical Management
The basic premise behind the nonsurgical management of these conditions involves a
period of rest until the player is asymptomatic followed by a return to throwing program.
Anti-inflammatory medications, ice, and other modalities may be useful. Injections, such
as corticosteroids and platelet-rich plasma (PRP), may be used in certain patients.
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
15/37

The following injuries warrant a trial of nonsurgical management because these players often
can RTS at a high rate:
Flexor-pronator or flexor-extensor strain
Medial/lateral epicondylitis
Little Leaguer’s elbow (medial apophysitis)
Olecranon stress reaction
Olecranon stress fracture
Persistent olecranon physis
Partial- or full-thickness UCL tear
Cubital tunnel syndrome
VEO
Medial epicondyle avulsion fracture without substantial displacement
Stable capitellar OCD
Radial tunnel syndrome
Contraindications
Acute, traumatic injuries that often warrant surgical management include:
Medial epicondyle fracture with substantial displacement
Olecranon fracture with displacement
Unstable OCD
Players in whom a reasonable course of nonsurgical treatment fails
Techniques/Procedures
Flexor-pronator or flexor-extensor strains are managed nonsurgically unless a complete
avulsion of the muscle origin is present.

Techniques/Procedures
Recovery from these injuries may be time-consuming, and often 2 to 3 months or more
may be required before the athlete is ready for game competition. Nonsurgical
management involves an approximately 6-week period of cessation from throwing until
the athlete is asymptomatic. During this time, the athlete should avoid activities that
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
16/37

cause pain. The use of a wrist splint may help athletes avoid activities that irritate the
muscle strain. Physical therapy to work on eccentric exercises should be initiated after
the pain has subsided. After the player is pain free, he or she can begin a return to
throwing program. Biologic injections, such as PRP, are not commonly offered but may
be considered in refractory cases or patients with more substantial strains. The use of
corticosteroids is avoided. Nonsurgical management is very successful, and most players
RTS within 3 months.
Players with medial or lateral epicondylitis initially are treated nonsurgically because
this particular pathology rarely necessitates surgical management.
Players with medial or lateral epicondylitis initially are treated with the use of a wrist
splint and physical therapy aimed at activating the problematic muscle group. Players
who are asymptomatic after 2 to 3 weeks of physical therapy can begin a return to
throwing program. Some studies have found corticosteroid injections to be effective with
regard to short-term pain relief; however, poorer outcomes often are observed at 1 year.
Therefore, the author of this lesson does not recommend corticosteroid injections. Data
regarding PRP injections, specifically leukocyte-rich PRP, are favorable for the
management of medial or lateral epicondylitis; therefore, PRP may be considered in
some patients. Nonsurgical management is very successful in returning these players to
sports activity. Patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails can undergo open or
arthroscopic débridement. Care must be taken during débridement to avoid damage to
the lateral UCL, which may result in elbow instability.
Athletes with Little Leaguer’s elbow are almost exclusively treated nonsurgically.
Players with medial apophysitis are treated via 4 to 6 weeks of cessation from throwing;
athletes may participate in physical therapy during this time but should avoid exercise
that stresses the medial elbow or causes pain. Athletes who are asymptomatic after 6
weeks can begin a gradual return to throwing program. Athletes who remain
symptomatic after 6 weeks are restricted from throwing until they are pain free.
Injections are not commonly indicated. Most players can successfully RTS.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
17/37

Patients with an olecranon stress reaction, olecranon stress fracture, or persistent
olecranon physis routinely undergo a trial of nonsurgical treatment, resulting in very
good success.
Players with an olecranon stress reaction, olecranon stress fracture, or persistent
olecranon physis should cease throwing for 6 weeks. Depending on the player’s pain
level with daily activities, a brief period of immobilization followed by physical therapy
may be considered to regain ROM. After the player is asymptomatic on physical
examination, a return to throwing program is initiated. Most players with a persistent
olecranon physis and olecranon stress reactions will respond well to nonsurgical
treatment. Often, nonsurgical treatment fails at a higher rate in players with an
olecranon stress fracture, especially if the fracture line is visible on plain radiographs.
Players in whom nonsurgical treatment fails are offered surgical treatment.
Patients, especially in younger athletes, with a partial- or full-thickness UCL tear often
undergo a trial of nonsurgical treatment.
If nonsurgical treatment fails, progression to UCL reconstruction or repair is indicated
if the player wants to RTS.
Partial- and full-thickness UCL tears often are initially managed nonsurgically.
Nonsurgical management of partial- and full-thickness tears is similar; however, the
timetable may be slightly longer for full-thickness tears. After the diagnosis is confirmed,
players should cease throwing for 6 to 8 weeks. During this time, they are permitted to
work on shoulder and elbow ROM and scapular mechanics and core strengthening but
should avoid stressing the medial elbow. After 6 to 8 weeks of no throwing, athletes are
reexamined. Athletes who are asymptomatic can begin a return to throwing program,
which they will progress through during the next several weeks. Athletes are permitted
to RTS after they have completed the throwing program. Interest in the use of biologic
augmentation for the management of these injuries has recently increased.
Unfortunately, data on to the advantages of PRP injection, the ideal composition of PRP
injections, the number of PRP injections, the postinjection protocol, are conflicting.
Therefore, the author of this lesson counsels patients on current data regarding biologic
augmentation rather than recommending for or against biologic augmentation. After the
patient and/or parent has all the available information, a mutual decision is made. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
18/37

success of nonsurgical management often is based on the tear location (proximal tears
result in better outcomes than distal tears) and tear severity (partial-thickness tears
result in better outcomes than full-thickness tears). Therefore, nonsurgical management
is more successful in for partial-thickness proximal tears than full-thickness distal tears.
Cubital tunnel syndrome may be difficult to manage nonsurgically, especially if it is a
dynamic phenomenon that affects players only during throwing.
Nonsurgical management consists of physical therapy to work on nerve glides and
mobilization and often is supplemented with a period of extension splinting at night.
This is attempted for 4 to 6 weeks; players who note improvement are permitted
to return to throwing.
Subcutaneous ulnar nerve transposition is indicated in patients who do not note
improvement.
Similar to partial-thickness UCL tears, VEO is managed via a period of cessation from
throwing followed by a return to throwing program.
A corticosteroid injection may be beneficial.
PRP is not used unless a concomitant UCL tear is present.
Patients who have a medial epicondyle avulsion fracture without substantial
displacement can be treated with the use of a splint for a short period followed by
progressive elbow mobilization.
Medial epicondyle avulsion fractures that are nondisplaced are initially managed via
immobilization. Extremes of elbow motion and maximal wrist extension and active wrist
flexion are avoided for the first several weeks to decrease stress on the medial
epicondyle. Repeat imaging studies, including radiographs and/or MRIs, can be obtained
to confirm the medial epicondyle has not displaced further. Athletes who are
asymptomatic on physical examination can begin a return to throwing program.
Stable capitellar OCD: early-stage capitellar OCD lesions in skeletally immature
athletes respond very well to nonsurgical management.
This is a common problem observed in overhead athletes and gymnasts.
Often, MRI will show separation of cartilage from the capitellum and chondral
fissuring.
Often, these patients must avoid throwing for 3 months or more, 6 months or
more may be necessary before return to throwing without pain.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:50 AM
AAOS | Throwing Elbow Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000029
19/37

During the initial rest phase, no weight bearing through the elbow and no throwing
are permitted.
Players with painless ROM of the elbow and imaging studies that do not show
progression of disease are permitted to return to throwing.
Radial tunnel syndrome is an uncommon entity and often improves with a brief
period of rest, with or without a corticosteroid injection.
Surgical Management
Indications
Surgical treatment often is indicated in throwing athletes with an elbow injury in whom a
course of nonsurgical treatment, including rest and rehabilitation, fails and who want to RTS at
the same or a higher level.
Some injuries, including medial epicondyle fractures with considerable displacement,
olecranon fractures with displacement, and unstable OCD, often are managed surgically
without a trial of nonsurgical management.
Contraindications
Players who do not want to continue as a throwing athlete and do not have symptoms with
other activities outside of throwing
Can consider position change
Techniques/Procedures: UCLR

has a palmaris longus to avoid erroneous harvest). Hamstring autograft and allograft are

Positioning
Supine on a hand table
If concomitant elbow arthroscopy is necessary, the arm can be brought across the chest, or
the patient can be placed in the sloppy lateral decubitus position and laid on the back, with a
hand table used for the UCL portion of the procedure.
Surgical Approach(es)
The surgeon can choose to split or elevate the flexor-pronator mass to access the native UCL.
The native UCL is then split in line with its fibers, and the sublime tubercle (ulna) and medial
epicondyle are located.
A tunnel with a 1-cm bone bridge that is 5 to 10 mm distal to the joint line is then created,
centered on the sublime tubercle.
The graft is passed through the tunnel after one end has been prepped with high-tensile
sutures.
A blind-ended socket is drilled at the origin of the UCL on the medial epicondyle, and two small
exit holes are drilled for suture passage.
One end of the graft is passed into the socket and excess length is removed from the opposite
end of the graft. The nonprepped end of the graft is then prepped with high-tensile sutures.
The second limb is then docked into the humerus, and the sutures used to prep the graft are
tied over a bone bridge with the elbow in approximately 60° of flexion and a varus stress
placed on the elbow (Figure 5).
If the ulnar nerve is transposed, this is completed now in a subcutaneous manner.
The incision is closed in a layered fashion.

Positioning
Supine on a hand table or in the lateral decubitus position with a bean bag
Surgical Approach(es)
A skin incision is made, centered over the fracture site.
Dissection is taken down to the fracture, taking care to avoid the ulnar nerve posteriorly and
the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve anteriorly.
The fracture is then exposed and cleaned out.
A traction suture is then placed in the flexor-pronator mass in a Krakow fashion to help control
the piece.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
After the piece is reduced, a guidewire is used to maintain reduction, and reduction is
confirmed fluoroscopically.
This guidewire should be placed in the center of the fracture fragment, up the humeral shaft,
avoiding the olecranon fossa.
After adequate reduction is confirmed, a second guidewire is placed to prevent rotation during
screw insertion.
Guidewire trajectory is confirmed fluoroscopically.
A cannulated drill for the 4.5-mm screw is then used to drill past the fracture fragment after
the length of the screw has been measured.
A 4.5-mm partially threaded cannulated screw with a washer is then used to fix the fracture.
Final reduction is confirmed fluoroscopically and radiographically (Figure 6).

A CT scan will provide critical information on the location of the posteromedial osteophyte.

Positioning
Lateral decubitus, prone, or supine with the arm over the body
Surgical Approach(es)
This can be performed in an arthroscopic or an open fashion.
An arthroscopic approach often is preferred to limit scar tissue formation.
Standard elbow arthroscopy is performed, with initial evaluation of the anterior elbow.
Débridement may be required in some patients.
Attention is then turned to the posterior elbow, and standard posterior and posterolateral
portals are made.
A burr or shaver is then used to resect the posteromedial osteophyte. Resection is taken down
to native bone, with great care taken to avoid over-resection because it may destabilize the
elbow of a throwing athlete.
Postoperative Care
The patient’s elbow is placed in a soft dressing, and immediate ROM is permitted.
Physical therapy is initiated to regain ROM followed by strength.
A throwing program often is initiated at approximately 2 to 3 months postoperatively, with
return to full competition at approximately 4 to 5 months postoperatively.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Understand the geometry of the osteophyte and the location at which pathologic anatomy
ends and normal bone begins to avoid over-resection and subsequent elbow instability.

Although uncommon, nonunion is possible with surgical management of olecranon fractures
and medial epicondyle fractures.

Nonunion
The type of nonunion (atrophic, hypertrophic, or oligotrophic) must be understood to
determine the appropriate next step. In patients with an atrophic nonunion, the problem
often is biologic; therefore, revision with biologic augmentation in the form of bone graft,
PRP, etc., should be considered. In patients with a hypertrophic nonunion, the problem
often is stability; therefore, revision surgery should attempt to stabilize the fracture
more appropriately.
Malunion
This may result from malreduction at the time of surgery or after displacement in athletes who
undergo open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) for the management of olecranon or
medial epicondyle fractures.
Patient symptoms dictate the need for additional treatment.
Pain
Residual pain is possible in all patients who undergo surgical treatment.
Although this is not a common finding, some areas of the elbow may become hypersensitive.
Infection
The blood supply to the upper extremity often is very good; therefore, infection is not a
common problem in this patient population.
If an infection occurs, it should be managed immediately via antibiotic agents or incision and
débridement.
The type and extent of infection often dictate management.

Although uncommon, fractures have been reported after UCLR.
Fractures often are managed via ORIF with the use of screws or suture anchors.
Hardware Failure
This may occur in patients with a delayed union or nonunion.
If hardware fails and the patient is symptomatic, the hardware should be removed, and
additional fixation should be provided.
Re-tear
Although uncommon, re-tear after UCLR is possible, and revision UCLR may be required.
Stiffness
Elbows managed surgically are at considerable risk for stiffness.

Stiffness
Elbow stiffness is common after elbow injury, especially in patients treated surgically.
This is especially true in patients with elbow trauma. Although other joints can be
immobilized for prolonged periods without considerable issue, prolonged
immobilization of the elbow may result in a completely different problem that needs to
be addressed. Stiffness may result from capsular contracture, muscle tightness, or
heterotopic ossification or may be iatrogenic from surgery. If the elbow begins to stiffen,
the patient should increase the frequency of physical therapy visits given that no bony
block to motion is present. Static progressive splinting and other techniques can be used
to help loosen the elbow.
Hematoma
This is an uncommon complication after elbow surgery. If substantial, it can be aspirated
under ultrasonographic guidance or may need to be evacuated.

Uncommon after elbow surgery
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
The ulnar nerve is the most common nerve affected during elbow surgery in throwing athletes.
Often, this is a transient neurapraxia resulting from traction on the nerve during surgery and
will resolve in several weeks.
The ulnar nerve may be damaged during surgery, which may result in considerable hand
dysfunction.
The ulnar nerve also is the most common nerve that can be injured during elbow arthroscopy.
The injury often is a transient neurapraxia.
Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation varies based on the type of injury and management.

Rehabilitation
For nonsurgically managed UCL tears—OCD, medial apophysitis, and cubital tunnel
syndrome—the player should cease throwing for 6 weeks and then undergo
reexamination. During these 6 weeks, the player works on hip and shoulder ROM and
scapular mechanics. If the physical examination maneuvers that were positive before the
cessation of throwing are negative after 6 weeks of throwing cessation, then a return to
throwing program is initiated and progressed accordingly.
For nonsurgically managed flexor-pronator strains—triceps tendinitis, medial and lateral
epicondylitis, and cubital tunnel syndrome—a similar approach is taken; however, the
player should cease throwing for only 4 weeks. Patients who are asymptomatic at follow-
up are permitted to begin a return to throwing program.
For nonsurgically managed olecranon stress fractures and reactions and medial
epicondyle fractures, the patient’s elbow typically is immobilized for a brief period before

the initiation of physical therapy to allow for bony healing. A return to throwing program
is initiated after a minimum of 6 to 8 weeks and after the athlete is pain free on physical
examination.
After UCLR or UCL repair, a brief period of immobilization is followed by physical therapy
to work on ROM and strengthening. This is followed by a return to throwing program,
which often begins approximately 3 months after UCL repair and 4.5 months after UCLR.
For all of these conditions, regardless whether managed surgically or nonsurgically,
physical therapy also must focus on proper pitching mechanics, core and lower body
strength, and many other fundamentals to ensure success. The pitching motion involves
the entire kinetic chain; therefore, a focus on all aspects of the thrower is essential.
After ORIF of a medial epicondyle or olecranon, the patient’s elbow is immobilized in a
splint for 7 to 10 days, after which ROM is progressed over the next 5 weeks.
Strengthening is begun at 6 weeks postoperatively, and a return to throwing program is
begun at approximately 4 months postoperatively, depending on how the player is
progressing.
Outcomes
The likelihood of RTS after the nonsurgical management of most elbow
strains/tendinitis/stress reactions is very good.
The RTS rate after ulnar nerve transposition in overhead athletes is 62%, with 56% of athletes
able to RTS at the same or a higher level.25
The RTS rate after ORIF of medial epicondyle fractures in throwing athletes is 73%, with 55% of
athletes able to RTS at the same or a higher level.26
The RTS rate after ORIF of olecranon fractures in throwing athletes is 67.5%, with 57.5% of
athletes able to RTS at the same or a higher level.27
Several studies have evaluated the ability of players of varying levels to RTS after UCLR and
UCL repair. Most have found that more than 80% of players can RTS at the same or a higher
level, with no substantial difference in performance metrics upon RTS28,29 (Resources 14 and
15).

Pearls and Pitfalls
Elbow injuries are common in throwing athletes.
A thorough patient history and a comprehensive physical examination are essential to
evaluate for deficiencies that may be contributing to increased stress on the elbow and to
prevent repeat injury in the future.
Advanced imaging studies of a thrower’s elbow often are abnormal.
Imaging study findings must be correlated with patient history and physical examination
findings to differentiate adaptive and pathologic MRI findings.
Many of these injuries can be initially managed nonsurgically.
Surgical treatment often is reserved for players in whom a course of nonsurgical treatment
fails and who want to RTS at a high level.
